definition:
The doctrine of assurance and perseverance asks two linked questions. Can a believer know that he belongs to God and will be saved at the last day? And will everyone who truly believes keep believing to the end? The New Testament answers the first with real promises meant to be trusted, such as “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). It answers the second with a double voice. On one side are promises that God keeps his people: “He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6). On the other are urgent warnings to hold fast and not fall away: “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). Every Christian tradition affirms both voices. They differ on how the promises and warnings fit together, and on whether a person who truly believed can finally be lost. This study traces both strands through Scripture; the related doctrines of election and justification have their own studies.

The vocabulary gathers around keeping and enduring. In Hebrew, God is the one who ‘keeps’ or ‘guards’ (shamar) his people (Psalm 121:4-8), and his chesed, his steadfast covenant love (the BSB renders it ‘loving devotion’), is the ground of their security. In Greek, hypomenō means ‘to remain under’ a load, and so ‘to endure’ or ‘persevere’ (Matthew 10:22), with the noun hypomonē, ‘endurance’. Menō, ‘to remain’ or ‘abide’, is John's word for continuing in Christ (John 15:4-7; 1 John 2:19). The language of assurance includes plērophoria, ‘full assurance’ or ‘full conviction’ (Hebrews 6:11; 10:22), and parrēsia, ‘confidence’ or ‘boldness’ (Hebrews 10:35). God's keeping is described with phroureō, a military word for guarding a city (1 Peter 1:5), and with phylassō, ‘to guard’ (Jude 24). The Spirit is the arrabōn, a commercial term for a first installment that guarantees the rest (Ephesians 1:14; 2 Corinthians 1:22). The words for falling away include parapiptō (Hebrews 6:6) and aphistēmi, ‘to withdraw’ or ‘turn away’ (Luke 8:13; Hebrews 3:12).
ot:
The Old Testament grounds security in the faithfulness of God, not in the steadiness of his people. The patriarchs receive promises God swears to keep: to Jacob, fleeing his brother, he says, “I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you” (Genesis 28:15). Moses tells Israel and Joshua that the LORD “will never leave you nor forsake you” (Deuteronomy 31:6, 8), a line Hebrews 13:5 applies to believers. Samuel, rebuking Israel for demanding a king, still assures them that “for the sake of His great name, the LORD will not abandon His people, because He was pleased to make you His own” (1 Samuel 12:22). God's choice is rooted in his own pleasure and name, and so it outlasts their failures.

Yet the same passages carry warnings. Samuel's next words are, “But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away” (1 Samuel 12:25). The covenant at Sinai set blessing and curse before Israel (Deuteronomy 28), and Moses calls them to “serve Him and hold fast to Him” (Deuteronomy 13:4). Israel's history is full of those who began well and turned aside. The wilderness generation, rescued from Egypt, died without entering the land because of unbelief, a story Psalm 95 retells and Hebrews 3 and 4 press on Christian readers. Solomon, who built the temple and prayed its great prayer, turned in old age after other gods, “his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice” (1 Kings 11:9). Ezekiel faces the case directly: “if a righteous man turns from his righteousness and practices iniquity,” none of his former righteousness will be remembered (Ezekiel 18:24). The Old Testament does not resolve the tension between these texts; it sets them side by side and trusts God to be faithful.

The Psalms and the Prophets give the promises their most personal voice. The pilgrim songs sing of a God who “will not allow your foot to slip” and who neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:3-4), and of those who trust him as “like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever” (Psalm 125:1). A psalmist who nearly lost his faith watching the wicked prosper confesses, “Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand” (Psalm 73:23), and “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26). Another prays, “The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me” (Psalm 138:8). Isaiah's God, answering Zion's complaint that she has been forgotten, says that a mother might forget her nursing child, “Even if she could forget, I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). In the rubble of Jerusalem the author of Lamentations remembers that “His mercies never fail” (Lamentations 3:22). The prophets then promise that God will do inwardly what the old covenant could not secure. Jeremiah hears God promise an everlasting covenant: “I will never turn away from doing good to them, and I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me” (Jeremiah 32:40). Ezekiel promises a new heart and God's own Spirit, who will “cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). Many interpreters see in these promises the Old Testament root of the doctrine that God preserves his people, since God himself undertakes to keep them from turning away.
nt:
Jesus speaks both ways. He warns that the love of many will grow cold, “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13). In the parable of the sower some receive the word with joy but have no root, and “They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away” (Luke 8:13). In John 15 he tells his disciples, “Remain in Me, and I will remain in you” (John 15:4), and warns that a branch that does not remain is thrown away and burned (John 15:6). Yet the same Gospel of John contains his strongest promises. “Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37); it is the Father's will “that I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day” (John 6:39). Of his sheep he says, “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand” (John 10:28). He prays for his followers, “Holy Father, protect them by Your name” (John 17:11), and before Peter's denial he tells him, “I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail” (Luke 22:32). Peter did fail that night, and he was restored (John 21:15-19). Judas, one of the Twelve, did not return.

Paul builds assurance on God's purpose and Christ's work. Romans 8 moves from God's foreknowledge through calling, justification, and glory as a chain in which no link is lost (Romans 8:29-30), and ends by asking, “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35), answering that nothing “in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). Christ intercedes for his people (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25). God “will sustain you to the end” (1 Corinthians 1:8), and believers are sealed with the Spirit “for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30). Assurance is also inward: “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children” (Romans 8:16). Yet Paul, too, warns. He tells Gentile believers that the natural branches were broken off because of unbelief and that they will be cut off unless they continue in God's kindness (Romans 11:20-22). He tells the Colossians they will be presented blameless “if indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm” (Colossians 1:23). He disciplines himself lest he be “disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27), and tells the Corinthians, “the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12), with the promise in the next verse that God is faithful and will provide a way to endure. He tells the Galatians that those seeking justification by the law “have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4). And he holds the two voices in a single sentence: “continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (Philippians 2:12-13).

The letter to the Hebrews contains the sharpest warnings in the Bible. It warns against drifting away (Hebrews 2:1), against “a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God” (Hebrews 3:12), and says, “We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first” (Hebrews 3:14). Hebrews 6:4-6 says it is impossible for those who have been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift, have shared in the Holy Spirit, and then have fallen away, to be restored to repentance, and Hebrews 10:26-29 speaks of a fearful expectation of judgment for those who trample the Son of God underfoot. Yet the writer immediately adds, “we are convinced of better things in your case—things that accompany salvation” (Hebrews 6:9), and grounds hope in God's oath, “an anchor for the soul, firm and secure” (Hebrews 6:19). He tells them, “You need to persevere” (Hebrews 10:36), and then, “we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls” (Hebrews 10:39). The general letters keep both notes. Believers are those “who through faith are shielded by God's power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time” (1 Peter 1:5), and they are to “strive to make your calling and election sure” (2 Peter 1:10). John says of those who left the church, “if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us” (1 John 2:19), and he writes so that believers “may know” they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). Jude tells his readers to “keep yourselves in the love of God” (Jude 21) and ends by praising “Him who is able to keep you from stumbling” (Jude 24). Paul at the end of his life can say, “I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7), and the risen Christ promises the churches, “Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10).

keyTexts.why: The LORD will not abandon his people for his name's sake, and yet persistent evil will sweep them away. Promise and warning in one speech.
A believer who nearly slipped confesses that God holds his right hand and is his portion forever. Assurance learned in the middle of doubt.
In the everlasting covenant God promises to put his fear in their hearts so that they will never turn away from him. The prophetic root of God's preserving grace.
Some believe for a season and fall away in testing; others hold the word fast and bear fruit with endurance. Jesus' own picture of persevering and failing faith.
No one can snatch Christ's sheep out of his hand or the Father's hand. The strongest promise of divine keeping in the Gospels.
Remain in me, Jesus says, and a branch that does not remain is thrown away. The call to abide, with its warning.
God's purpose runs from foreknowledge to glory, and nothing in creation can separate believers from his love in Christ. The great text of assurance.
Gentile believers stand by faith and must not be arrogant, for they too can be cut off if they do not continue in God's kindness. Paul's warning within his argument about Israel.
God will complete the good work he began. Assurance grounded in God's commitment rather than the believer's strength.
Work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for God is at work in you. Human effort and divine working in one sentence.
The most debated warning in the New Testament, followed at once by the writer's confidence of better things. Every view of perseverance must account for it.
Hold fast, do not throw away your confidence, you need endurance, and we are not of those who shrink back. Exhortation, warning, and assurance together.
An imperishable inheritance is kept in heaven for those who are guarded by God's power through faith. God guards, and faith is the means.
Those who left did not belong, for if they had, they would have remained. A key text for reading apostasy as revealing rather than reversing.
Keep yourselves in the love of God, and praise to him who is able to keep you from stumbling. Jude's letter ends on both halves of the doctrine.

history:
The early church spoke far more of endurance than of assurance. Living under intermittent persecution, it honored martyrs and grieved over those who lapsed, and the persecution under the emperor Decius around AD 250 forced Cyprian of Carthage and the church at Rome to decide whether the lapsed could be restored, which they allowed after penance. The Shepherd of Hermas (second century) debated whether there could be repentance after baptism. Augustine of Hippo gave the West its classic account. In On Rebuke and Grace (426 or 427) and On the Gift of Perseverance (428 or 429) he taught that perseverance to the end is a distinct gift of God, given to the elect; he also held that some who were truly baptized and justified do not receive that gift and fall away, and that no one in this life can know with certainty whether he is among the elect. The Council of Orange (529, canon 10) taught that even the regenerate must always seek God's help to persevere. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 109, article 10) likewise held that the one in grace needs the further help of God to persevere to the end.

The Reformation made assurance a central question. Luther and Calvin taught that faith itself carries confidence in God's mercy, and Calvin defined faith as a firm and certain knowledge of God's goodwill toward us, founded on the promise given in Christ (Institutes 3.2.7, 1559), while insisting that faith is always assailed by doubt. Calvin taught that the elect will persevere (Institutes 3.24). The Lutheran Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 12) condemned the Anabaptists who denied that those once justified can lose the Holy Spirit, and Lutheran theology has held that believers can fall from grace while directing them to seek assurance in Christ, the Word, and the sacraments. The Council of Trent, in its decree on justification (session 6, 1547), taught that perseverance is a great gift of God (chapter 13), that grace is lost by mortal sin and restored through penance, and that no one can know with absolute certainty that he will persevere unless he learns it by special revelation (canon 16). The followers of Jacobus Arminius, in the Remonstrance of 1610 (Article 5), affirmed that Christ keeps believers from falling through the power of his grace but left open whether believers could fall away through negligence, calling for further study of Scripture; within a few years the Remonstrants were teaching that they could. The Synod of Dort (1618 to 1619), in the fifth head of its Canons, answered that God preserves true believers so that they cannot totally and finally fall away, and that they gain assurance from faith in God's promises, the testimony of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), and a serious pursuit of a good conscience and good works. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapters 17 and 18) and the Baptist Second London Confession (1689) followed Dort, adding that assurance is not of the essence of faith, so that a true believer may wait long and struggle hard before attaining it.

The English Puritans wrote at length for troubled consciences. William Perkins (1558 to 1602) and later writers such as Thomas Brooks, whose Heaven on Earth (1654) is a treatise on assurance, counseled believers to look to Christ and to the evidences of grace, and critics then and since have worried that the search for evidences turned believers inward. John Wesley's experience at Aldersgate Street on 24 May 1738, when he felt his heart strangely warmed and received an assurance that Christ had taken away his sins, shaped a Methodist teaching on the witness of the Spirit (his sermons on the subject date from 1746 and 1767), while his Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints (1751) argued that a believer can fall away and perish. In the twentieth century John Owen's older reading of Hebrews as describing those who never truly believed was joined by other approaches: Robert Shank's Life in the Son (1960) and I. Howard Marshall's Kept by the Power of God (1969) defended the real possibility of apostasy; Thomas Schreiner and Ardel Caneday's The Race Set Before Us (2001) read the warnings as the means God uses to preserve believers. In American evangelicalism the lordship salvation controversy set John MacArthur's The Gospel According to Jesus (1988) against Zane Hodges's Absolutely Free (1989), with Charles Ryrie's So Great Salvation (1989) also rejecting what MacArthur's critics called lordship salvation. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) affirms that all true believers endure to the end, a position held by many Baptists who do not share the Reformed doctrine of election. Four Views on Eternal Security (2002), edited by J. Matthew Pinson, sets out classical Calvinist, moderate Calvinist, Reformed Arminian, and Wesleyan views. The site's page on how we are saved surveys the wider debate.

differ.body: God who began the work will finish it. Those whom God has chosen, called, justified, and regenerated by his Spirit will certainly persevere in faith to the end, not because of their strength but because God keeps them, Christ intercedes for them, and the Spirit seals them (John 10:28-29; Romans 8:29-39; Philippians 1:6). True believers can fall into serious sin and backslide for a time, as Peter did, but they cannot totally and finally fall away. Those who do fall away show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). The warnings in Hebrews are real and are addressed to the whole visible church; God uses them as means to keep his people alert and persevering, so that the warnings and promises work together. Assurance is available to believers through God's promises, the witness of the Spirit, and the fruit of grace, though it may be weak or clouded for a time.

God's grace is strong enough to keep every believer, and no outside power can snatch them from Christ's hand. But a believer remains a person in a real relationship, and the New Testament's warnings describe a real danger: a true believer can turn away from Christ in unbelief and be finally lost (Hebrews 3:12-14; 6:4-6; 10:26-29; Colossians 1:23). The warnings would be empty if they described something that could never happen to their readers. Wesleyans hold that a person who falls away may be restored through repentance, and they stress the Spirit's direct witness to believers that they are God's children. Reformed Arminians, such as Robert Picirilli and Stephen Ashby, hold that apostasy happens only through a decisive turning from faith and, on their reading of Hebrews 6:4-6, cannot be reversed. Both hold that believers can have present assurance while they continue in faith.

Lutherans confess that salvation is wholly God's gift and that God's election in Christ is a comfort to troubled consciences, yet they also teach, with the Augsburg Confession, that those once justified can lose the Holy Spirit and fall from grace through unbelief or deliberate sin. They refuse to resolve this in either direction by logic. Assurance is not sought by examining one's own perseverance or searching God's hidden decree but by looking outward to Christ as he gives himself in the preached Word, in baptism, and in the Lord's Supper. The baptized believer who falls away is called back to his baptism, God's promise that still stands. Lutherans see the Reformed and Arminian systems alike as attempts to explain what Scripture leaves as the paradox of grace.

Salvation begins and continues by grace, and final perseverance is a great gift of God that no one can merit. The justified person truly receives the life of grace, can grow in it, and can lose it through mortal sin, a grave and deliberate turning from God; it is restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance. Christians should have firm hope and confidence in God's mercy, but, as the Council of Trent taught, no one can know with absolute certainty that he will persevere to the end without a special revelation. Catholic teaching holds that this guards against presumption on one side and despair on the other, keeping the believer in humble trust and active love. Defenders point to Paul's warnings, his own discipline lest he be disqualified (1 Corinthians 9:27), and the call to work out salvation with fear and trembling.

differ.view: Eternal security without necessary perseverance (Free Grace)
differ.body: Some evangelical theologians, such as Zane Hodges and Charles Ryrie, hold that eternal life is given the moment a person believes in Christ and can never be lost, because it is a free gift and God does not take back his gifts. They argue that making final salvation depend on a life of persevering obedience brings works back in by the side door and robs believers of assurance, since no one's obedience is complete. On this view a true believer will normally show fruit, but a genuine believer may fall into a carnal life and still be saved, and Hodges held that this remains true even of one who later stops believing. The warnings of Hebrews and similar passages are read as threats of God's discipline in this life or loss of reward at the judgment seat of Christ (1 Corinthians 3:12-15), not loss of salvation. Critics in every other tradition hold that this view separates faith from repentance and obedience in a way the New Testament does not.

errors:
The church has rejected two opposite distortions. The first is presumption: the idea that a person can claim salvation while living in settled rebellion against God, because of a past decision, a religious ceremony, or membership in a church. Jesus warned of those who call him Lord and do not do the Father's will (Matthew 7:21-23), and Paul and Hebrews warn professing believers who are drifting. The Reformers insisted that faith is never alone, and even those who hold that a true believer can never be lost agree that assurance does not belong to someone who has no concern for holiness. The second distortion is despair or perpetual anxiety: the belief that no one can ever rest in God's promises, that assurance is always pride, or that the Christian life is a test one is always about to fail. That turns the good news into a new burden and contradicts John, who wrote so that believers may know they have eternal life (1 John 5:13).

Subtler errors follow. Assurance can be grounded in the wrong place, in the strength of one's feelings, the intensity of one's commitment, or a remembered moment, rather than in Christ and God's promise. Perseverance can be treated as a human achievement that earns final salvation, when every tradition agrees it is sustained by grace. And the warnings can be read as if they belonged only to someone else, the weaker brother or the other tradition, when the New Testament addresses them to the whole church, the writers included (1 Corinthians 9:27).
life:
The doctrine meets people at two very different points. Some are careless and need the warnings: faith is not a ticket punched once, and a life that drifts from Christ is in real danger. Others are anxious, and they need the promises: the one who comes to Christ will not be driven away (John 6:37), and the God who began the work will finish it. Wise pastors across the traditions have known that the same sermon can crush the tender and comfort the careless if the wrong half is heard, and that the cure for both is to look away from oneself to Christ, who holds his people and intercedes for them.

Perseverance is also a community practice. Hebrews does not tell isolated believers to hold on; it tells them to “exhort one another daily” (Hebrews 3:13) and not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25). People who are struggling to keep believing are kept, in part, by others who pray for them and do not let them go, as Jesus prayed for Peter before his fall. And endurance is not a steady mood. The psalmist who confessed that God held his right hand did so after nearly slipping (Psalm 73:2, 23). Doubt, weariness, and seasons of dryness are not proof that a person has fallen away; the question is where they turn.
questions: Jesus says no one can snatch his sheep from his hand (John 10:28) and also warns that a branch that does not remain will be thrown away (John 15:6). How do the traditions described here hold these sayings together, and which account seems most faithful to both?
According to the New Testament, where should a believer look for assurance, and what goes wrong when assurance is sought mainly in feelings or in one's own track record?
Hebrews calls believers to exhort one another daily so that none is hardened by sin. What would it look like for a church to take shared responsibility for one another's perseverance?
